Not exactly. Each time a cell divides it loses some of its telomeres. When there are no more telomeres in a cell's DNA it dies or deactivates itself, loss of healthy cells equals decline in health and function and eventually death. This would effectively be an upper limit to human longevity, my guess is somewhere around 120 years.

http://learn.genetics.utah.edu/content/basics/telomeres/

In white blood cells, the length of telomeres ranges from 8,000 base pairs in newborns to 3,000 base pairs in adults and as low as 1,500 in elderly people. (An entire chromosome has about 150 million base pairs.) Each time it divides, an average cell loses 30 to 200 base pairs from the ends of its telomeres.

Certain cancers produce telomerase to allow cancerous cells to divide more times than would otherwise be possible. Care would have to be taken when manipulating telomere length to extend lifespan so as not to create cancerous (or cancer-like?) cells in the process.
